name: Мат турою за два ходи
description:
By now you have practiced mating with the queen several times. Matting with the rook is more difficult. Because the rook only moves straight and not diagonally, it is more difficult to take flight spaces from the enemy king. Strong cooperation between rook and king is vital.

In order to mate with the rook, it is important to know what to work towards. In examples 1 and 2, you see checkmate images in which the other's king is at the edge or in the corner. Note that in both cases the kings are in opposition to each other.

In examples 3-7, white gives mate in two.

In examples 3-5, the black king only has one possible move. We see how white can respond to this in various ways. Here we are appplying the concept of zugzwang with a waiting move.

In examples 6 and 7, the black king has more escape squares, but white is able to mate there too, by strategically positioning their king.

What do you have to do?

Give mate in two with the rook. If the defender's king is on the edge, make sure your king faces the other one move before the checkmate. A check on the edge on which the defending king stands then leads to mate.

examples.text: The black king stands at the edge and the kings face each other. The white king controls all the squares on the g-file. With a check on the h-file, white takes away the squares on the h-file. Checkmate!

The black king stands in the corner and the kings face each other. The white king thus takes away all the squares on the seventh row. With a check on the eighth row, white takes away the squares on the eighth row. Checkmate!

Note that here, with a king on g6, white also takes away all the squares on the seventh row. So with a defending king in the corner, it is not necessary to have the kings face each other to give mate. However, of course, the attacking king must be near the defending king to take away all the escape squares that the rook cannot take away.

The defending king is on the edge. Giving check does not make sense yet, because the king can then flee to a7. First white has to take away squares a7 and b7 with the king. Then a check with the rook is sufficient for mate: 1.Kb6 Kb8 (the kings face each other) 2.Rd8#.

This is a very important situation. Chess is a game in which both players must take turns to make a move. Were a player allowed to skip a turn at a time that suits them, then (when the defending king is not in the corner) you would never be able to mate with king and rook against king, for example.

Take a look at this example. With a defending king at the edge, the kings must face each other in order to mate. However, if white now puts the king opposite the black one, the black king runs away and white can start again. But wait! What if it is black's turn now? Then they must move the king one step to the side after which the kings do face each other. Then playing the rook to the eighth row is immediate mate. 

Yet white can do something very clever here. White is going to put black into zugzwang. Zugzwang means that a player has to play a move, which they actually do not want to play. The reason is that they have no other suitable options.

Here we see that black's only move 1...Kg8 leads to mate. By continuing to control the e-file with the rook and leaving the king on g6, black has a problem. With a waiting move, white puts black in a bind: 1.Re5 (1.Re4/3/2/1 work just as well) 1...Kg8 2.Re8#.

Again, the king has only one possible move. It is good to anticipate this. After 1...Kh2 you would actually want to give mate with 2.Rh4+, but then the king can still move to g1. Logical, because the kings don't face each other! Now it is simple. White starts with 1.Kf2 and after 1...Kh2 the kings do face each other. The escape squares on the g-file are taken away by the white king. Now it is time to finish it off: 2.Rh4#.

Compared to the previous examples, the black king now has more space. With the following move, white keeps the black king at the edge and at the same time causes black to have to move the king opposite the white one. The next move is mate: 1.Kb6 Kb8 2.Rd8#

The black king is on the edge, so we want to keep it that way. As in the previous example, white takes away two out of the three escaping squares and at the same time forces black to move their king opposite the white one on the next move. The next move is mate: 1.Rd7 Ka5 2.Ra7#.
